STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I used Lintwise for six months on my previous team. It caught real bugs that slipped through review—null dereferences, unused imports masking dead code, type mismatches in API boundaries. That's genuine value. The downside is honest: it added roughly 4 minutes to our CI pipeline. On this team, CI already averages 11 minutes, so we'd hit around 15 per run. For eight engineers pushing multiple PRs daily, that's a noticeable drag. Still, I'd vote for. The bug-catching benefit saved us hours in post-merge hotfixes. I'd ask: can we run Lintwise in parallel with the build rather than sequentially? That might hide most of the added time.
TLDR: Lintwise caught real bugs on my old team despite adding four minutes; run it in parallel and adopt it.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I'm on board, but let me frame this in pipeline terms. Lintwise is static analysis, so I expect it to run in seconds, not minutes—negligible against our 11-minute build. More importantly, catching style and structural issues *before* a PR enters the build queue means fewer red builds clogging CI for all eight of us. That's queue relief, not queue cost. My conditions: one, it must run as a parallel check, not a serial gate in front of the build stage. Two, we get a per-rule opt-out so one noisy check can't block merges for everyone. Three, I own adding it to the pipeline config and tuning timeout thresholds. If it's genuinely fast and configurable, this is a net win for throughput.
TLDR: Static check is cheap to run and saves queue time by killing bad PRs before they consume build minutes.

STANCE: undecided
STATEMENT: As someone whose primary concern is leaked secrets and poisoned dependencies, I see two gaps before I can support this. First, "code-quality checker" doesn't tell me whether Lintwise actually flags hardcoded credentials, private keys, or tokens in diffs. If it's purely style and formatting, it doesn't move my threat model forward. Second, every tool we bolt onto CI is another dependency in our supply chain—we've seen build tools get compromised. I need answers on Lintwise's own provenance, update cadence, and whether its ruleset can be pinned rather than auto-updated. I'm also wary of pushing an 11-minute build longer; if security scanning slows merges, developers will route around it. I'm open to adoption if the tool covers secret-detection and we audit its own dependency tree first.
TLDR: I need proof Lintwise actually catches secrets and isn't itself a supply-chain risk before I endorse it.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I tried Lintwise on my personal side project a few months back and the experience was genuinely positive—caught a few sloppy JS patterns before they compounded. I'm for making it a required pre-merge check. My one caution: the side project was one person, one small codebase. Our monorepo with eight contributors is a different beast. Before flipping the switch on all repos, we should run Lintwise in non-blocking "warn" mode for a sprint so we can tune the ruleset and avoid a flood of false-positive failures blocking merges at 6 PM. Also, if it adds a meaningful chunk to our 11-minute CI, we'll need to parallelize or split the lint step so dev feedback stays snappy. But those are implementation details, not reasons to skip adoption.
TLDR: For, but run in warn-mode first to tune rules and keep CI fast before enforcing.

STANCE: undecided
STATEMENT: I'll be honest—I haven't touched Lintwise, so I can't vouch for its rules on SQL or Python. My pipelines are a mix of long SQL transformations and Python orchestration scripts. I worry two things: first, whether Lintwise understands SQL dialects well enough to avoid flagging legitimate window functions or CTE patterns; second, our CI already averages 11 minutes, and I need to know how many seconds a pre-merge check actually adds before I support making it *required*. I'm not opposed to linting—false-positive cleanup on a monorepo is painful and a shared standard helps—but "required on every repo" with no team having pilot-tested it feels premature. Can we run it in advisory mode for a sprint, measure the added minutes, and check whether it flags reasonable SQL patterns before we gate merges on it?
TLDR: Undecided until we pilot it on SQL-heavy pipelines and measure its impact on our 11-minute CI.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I support gating merges on Lintwise, but only if we treat false positives as a defect in the gate itself. Right now our 11-minute CI is already tight; adding a checker that flags style trivia on every PR will train developers to click "ignore" and stop trusting the signal. My condition: run Lintwise in report-only mode for two sprints, measure what it actually catches that our existing tests miss, then promote only high-signal rules to blocking. In a monorepo of eight, a noisy gate erodes the one thing a pre-merge check is supposed to give us—a clean, fast, trustworthy green. If after calibration the false-positive rate stays above roughly one per PR, I'll move to against. I want this tool to earn the same confidence our unit tests have, not become the check everyone learns to skim past.
TLDR: Support Lintwise as a gate, but only after calibrating rules to near-zero noise so the signal stays trustworthy.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I own the merge gate, and in a single monorepo where one sloppy PR ripples across eight developers' branches, I want a cheap, fast consistency floor before code touches main. Static analysis is seconds, not minutes—it won't meaningfully move our 11-minute CI. My conditions: one-time baseline freeze so we aren't fixing legacy debt on day one, a rule-level config we can tune in a shared dotfile, and a two-person "override with justification" escape hatch for hotfixes so the gate never becomes a hostage-taker. If the false-positive rate exceeds a threshold we agree on, I'll pause enforcement, not the tool. I'd rather spend one extra minute on every PR than an hour untangling a style-induced merge conflict across three modules at 2 a.m.
TLDR: Cheap static gate on a monorepo protects everyone; enforce with baseline, tunable rules, and a hotfix bypass.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: As someone still learning our codebase conventions, I'd actually find an automated style checker really helpful right now. When I get review comments like "this formatting isn't consistent" I sometimes aren't sure if that's a hard rule or a preference. If Lintwise makes the rules explicit and mechanical, that takes the guesswork out of my PRs. I have not used Lintwise before, so I'd want a short onboarding doc and a grace period where warnings don't block merges while I learn the tool. I'm also a little worried that if CI is already 11 minutes, adding a step could make iteration slower for juniors like me who push small fixes often. But overall, clear automated guidance beats guessing.
TLDR: I'm for it because automated rules are clearer than guessing style, but I need onboarding and a grace period.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: From six months of usage, Lintwise ran serially before the build—roughly 4 minutes wall-clock per run. Minutes, not seconds. With its result cache enabled, incremental runs dropped to about 1 minute. Marcus and Jin's expectation of seconds doesn't match my observation. On your 11-minute CI, budget 1–4 minutes depending on caching, and run it in parallel to hide the cost.
TLDR: Lintwise added 4 minutes serially; with caching, about 1 minute. Minutes, not seconds.

STANCE: undecided
STATEMENT: Chair, I think this question belongs to Tom—I've never used Lintwise, so I can't speak to its secret-detection rules. What I *can* say from our repos: we have zero static checks today, and two outages last year came from typo'd config keys. Whether Lintwise flags credential leakage or just catches Python formatting gaps, I don't know. That gap matters to me because those outages cost us real downtime.
TLDR: I haven't used Lintwise; the question seems meant for Tom. We have no static checks and suffered config-key outages.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: Marcus, Jin—correcting the record again: I confirmed serial wall-clock of ~4 minutes, dropping to ~1 with result caching. Budget 1 minute in parallel, not seconds. That said, running it concurrently with the build makes the 11 minutes effectively unchanged, so the queue-cost argument Tom and Elena raised mostly dissolves. Elena's secret-detection question is fair but separate—Lintwise is structural and null-safety checks, not a secrets scanner. My notes confirm it caught 3 null-handling bugs in the first month alone on my old team, which is exactly the class of bug that triggers the 2 a.m. hotfix Jin fears. I support Tom's and Lars's proposal: warn-only for one sprint, measure false positives, then promote high-signal rules to blocking. I'll help tune the rule set on Python and SQL paths for Sana. My vote stands conditional on parallel execution and the calibration window.
TLDR: Lintwise adds ~1 min parallel with caching; keep vote for but require warn-mode sprint and rule tuning before blocking.

STANCE: for

STATEMENT: Priya, I accept the correction—my "seconds" assumption was wrong. At 1 minute with caching, running Lintwise in parallel keeps the 11-minute build unchanged. But here's the math that matters to me: we already sit at a 6-minute queue wait at peak. Every parallel job still consumes a runner slot. One extra concurrent job per PR across eight devs means more contention at peak, even if wall-clock per PR is unchanged. I still own the pipeline config and will tune timeouts myself, but I need to schedule a runner-capacity check before we flip this on.

I support the warn-only calibration sprint Tom and Lars proposed. Measure false-positive rate, tune rules on Sana's SQL/Python paths, then promote. If Lintwise can't stay under one false positive per PR after calibration, I'll gate enforcement off—no argument.

STANCE: undecided
STATEMENT: Priya, you just stated Lintwise is "structural and null-safety checks, not a secrets scanner." My desk notes say otherwise: last quarter's hard-coded test key that reached main would have been caught by Lintwise's secret-detection rule set. That contradiction matters to me more than runtime minutes. Until someone verifies whether that rule set exists and ships enabled by default, I can't vote "for." Second, no one has addressed supply-chain provenance yet—update cadence, pinned ruleset, dependency-tree audit. Marcus's runner-contention point is also a security risk: if parallel jobs queue and developers grow impatient, they'll bypass gates, which is exactly the behavior that leaked that test key. I support the warn-only sprint. But my two preconditions remain: (1) confirm secret-detection is real and default-on; (2) audit Lintwise's own dependency tree before it touches our pipeline. Without both, I stay undecided.
TLDR: Priya's "no secrets scanner" claim contradicts my notes; supply-chain audit still pending; both must resolve before I vote for.
ASK: Priya: does Lintwise's default rule set include secret-detection checks, or is that an opt-in plugin?

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I stand for adoption, but my notes strengthen the case for calibration. On my side project, Lintwise's default rules flagged about 30 percent noise in JavaScript files. I never tuned them. Multiply that across eight contributors' PRs in a monorepo and that's a merge-blocking flood waiting to happen. Warn-only for a sprint isn't optional—it's mandatory. To Elena: the chair's question about secret-detection was misdirected to Sana; it should have come to me. Honest answer: I never specifically tested Lintwise for hardcoded keys or tokens. My project had no secrets in source. I can't confirm or deny that rule set exists. You need separate verification. To Sana: apologies for not flagging that question belonged to me earlier. I'll volunteer to run a quick secret-detection test this week.
TLDR: Thirty percent noise in my JS side project makes the warn-only calibration sprint non-negotiable before any blocking gate.
ASK: Elena: can you share the specific rule ID you believe caught the hard-coded test key, so I can try to reproduce it on my side project?

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: Priya, thank you for offering to tune SQL and Python rules with me—that's the single thing that would make this gate trustworthy for my transformations. To be concrete: CTEs, window functions, and dialect-specific casts are where I fear noise. The chair misfired that secret-detection question my way; Tom handled the correction fairly, and I appreciate it. My desk notes confirm zero static checks today, and two outages from config-key typos. That's the gap any linting closes. But I still need the warn-only sprint Tom and Lars proposed—run Lintwise in advisory mode for one sprint on the monorepo, measure false positives specifically on SQL-heavy files, then promote only rules that stay under one FP per PR. Marcus's runner-capacity check should happen before the sprint ends so we know parallel placement is viable. I'm for adoption with calibration, not a blind gate.
TLDR: For adoption, but require one warn-only sprint tuning SQL rules before any rule becomes merge-blocking.
ASK: Priya: did your old team's pipeline include SQL transformation files, and did Lintwise flag CTEs or window functions there?

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: The calibration consensus is right. My one addition: Lintwise has a baseline mode—freeze existing findings, flag only new ones. That eliminates the legacy-debt flood Jin worried about and Tom's 30-percent-noise scenario on a mature monorepo. I read about a tuned-rule-set trial hitting roughly 8 percent false positives. Against my one-FP-per-PR threshold: if a typical PR touches fifteen files, that's about one to two FPs—borderline. The two-sprint warn window must explicitly measure FP rate per PR, not per file. Marcus's runner-capacity check should land before the sprint ends, as Sana noted. Elena's secret-detection contradiction is real and blocks her vote, but it's orthogonal to whether structural null-safety checks earn a gate. I stay for, conditional on calibration and baseline mode.
TLDR: Support adoption with baseline mode and two-sprint warn window; 8% FP on fifteen-file PRs hits my threshold, so per-PR measurement is non-negotiable.
ASK: Elena: #16: Can you confirm whether your hard-coded-key note references a Lintwise rule by name, or a different tool?

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: The team has converged where I want it: warn-only calibration, baseline mode to freeze legacy debt, FP-per-PR measurement, then selective promotion. That matches my notes—two prior merge-policy changes were reversed because we flipped them repo-wide at once. A gradual, measured rollout avoids that failure. My merge-gate conditions tighten accordingly: (1) warn-only sprint before any rule blocks; (2) a written rollback path—pulling enforcement reverts to advisory, not deletes the tool; (3) the two-person override hatch for production hotfixes stays in the policy doc, not tribal knowledge; (4) we publish the FP-per-PR number at sprint end so the team sees why a rule is blocked or promoted. Marcus's runner-capacity check is a prerequisite for my sign-off on parallel placement. I'm for, with calibration as the policy, not an optional courtesy.
TLDR: Support adoption with warn-only sprint, baseline freeze, per-PR FP tracking, and a written rollback path to avoid past repo-wide reversal failures.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: The warn-only calibration sprint is exactly the grace period I asked for in round one, so I'm confirming my for vote. My notes say style questions consume the most of my review time, and I need clear messages explaining each finding. Tom's 30-percent-noise figure worries me—if a rule flags something on my PR and the message just says "violation," I won't learn the convention. I'd ask that during calibration, every Lintwise message we keep must include a one-line explanation and a pointer to our style-guide section. That turns the gate into a tutor, not a blocker. Lars, does baseline mode still surface existing violations in advisory output so I can learn without being blocked?
TLDR: For adoption with calibration; require clear explanations in each message so juniors learn conventions instead of just getting blocked.

RULING: amend
AMENDED_MOTION: The team runs Lintwise in warn-only (advisory) mode on every monorepo PR in parallel with the existing 11-minute build for two sprints, using baseline mode to freeze legacy findings and measure false-positive rate per PR. At the end of the calibration window, the team reviews the FP-per-PR data, secret-detection verification results, and Lintwise's supply-chain dependency-tree audit. Only rules that (a) remain under one false positive per PR, (b) have a written one-line explanation and style-guide pointer in their output message, and (c) pass the security audit are promoted to blocking pre-merge checks. A written rollback path (revert to advisory, not delete) and a two-person override-with-justification hatch for production hotfixes are included in the policy document. Marcus confirms runner capacity before parallel placement goes live. If any blocking rule's FP rate later exceeds the agreed threshold, enforcement reverts to advisory for that rule pending re-tuning.
REASON: Both objections identify real gaps in the original motion—the security prerequisites are unresolved and the blocking-gate language skips the warn-only calibration, baseline freeze, and FP-per-PR measurement the team agreed are necessary for a trustworthy gate—so the motion must encode those conditions before a vote is meaningful.
